Finally, an open-source implementation is offered, compatible with any counterfactual explanation generator algorithm. Code repository at: https://github.com/ADMAntwerp/CounterPlots

papers.title: InversionView: A General-Purpose Method for Reading Information from Neural Activations
papers.research_question: How can we decipher the information encoded in neural activations? The paper proposes InversionView, a method to sample from the preimage of an activation to uncover the information content.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces InversionView, a method that samples from the preimage of an activation via a conditional decoder to uncover the information encoded in neural activations and understand model algorithms.
papers.conclusion: InversionView is a general-purpose method that effectively deciphers information in neural activations, enabling better understanding of model algorithms and simplifying interpretability workflows.
papers.key_findings:
InversionView can reveal both basic and complex information in activations, such as token counts and relative positions.
InversionView simplifies interpretability workflows, agreeing with prior circuit findings in GPT-2 small.
InversionView enabled the first fully verified circuit for a 3-digit addition model.
InversionView scales to larger models like GPT-2 for factual recall.
papers.limitation:
Training a decoder requires a dataset of activations and can be computationally expensive.
The decoder may not perfectly capture the preimage, leading to potential biases in the generated samples.
The method is currently limited to discrete sequences (text).
future_direction: Extend InversionView to continuous domains.
Improve decoder efficiency.
Automate interpretation using LLMs.
papers.abstract: The inner workings of neural networks can be better understood if we can fully decipher the information encoded in neural activations. In this paper, we argue that this information is embodied by the subset of inputs that give rise to similar activations. We propose InversionView, which allows us to practically inspect this subset by sampling from a trained decoder model conditioned on activations. This helps uncover the information content of activation vectors, and facilitates understanding of the algorithms implemented by transformer models. We present four case studies where we investigate models ranging from small transformers to GPT-2. In these studies, we show that InversionView can reveal clear information contained in activations, including basic information about tokens appearing in the context, as well as more complex information, such as the count of certain tokens, their relative positions, and abstract knowledge about the subject. We also provide causally verified circuits to confirm the decoded information.

papers.title: Circular Reasoning: Understanding Self-Reinforcing Loops in Large Reasoning Models
papers.research_question: What is the 'Circular Reasoning' failure mode in Large Reasoning Models, and how can we systematically analyze its mechanisms and predict its onset?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies the 'Circular Reasoning' failure mode in Large Reasoning Models, introduces LoopBench for systematic evaluation, analyzes the mechanisms (state collapse, triggers, persistence via V-shaped attention), and proposes an early prediction method using CUSUM on hidden states.
papers.conclusion: Circular reasoning is a critical failure mode in LRMs that stems from intrinsic generation mechanisms, and the proposed analysis and prediction method provide a foundation for improving reasoning stability.
papers.key_findings:
Circular reasoning manifests as two distinct loop types: numerical loops (universal) and statement loops (prevalent in reasoning models).
LoopBench triggers significantly higher repetition rates than existing benchmarks, revealing model fragility.
The loop onset is triggered by reasoning impasses and sustained by a self-reinforcing V-shaped attention pattern.
Early prediction of statement loops is feasible by monitoring hidden state shifts with the CUSUM algorithm.
Decoding strategies mitigate but do not eliminate repetition, indicating an inherent trade-off between loop and accuracy.
papers.limitation:
LoopBench focuses on specific task patterns (high-precision arithmetic and complex recursive reasoning) and may not cover all reasoning scenarios.
The early prediction method is only validated for statement loops, not numerical loops.
The analysis is primarily conducted on open-source models, limiting generalizability to closed-source models.
future_direction: Expand LoopBench to more diverse tasks and domains.
Investigate loop mitigation strategies, such as dynamic decoding or architectural modifications.
Extend the analysis to more model architectures and scales.
papers.abstract: Despite the success of test-time scaling, Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) frequently encounter repetitive loops that lead to computational waste and inference failure. In this paper, we identify a distinct failure mode termed Circular Reasoning. Unlike traditional model degeneration, this phenomenon manifests as a self-reinforcing trap where generated content acts as a logical premise for its own recurrence, compelling the reiteration of preceding text. To systematically analyze this phenomenon, we introduce LoopBench, a dataset designed to capture two distinct loop typologies: numerical loops and statement loops. Mechanistically, we characterize circular reasoning as a state collapse exhibiting distinct boundaries, where semantic repetition precedes textual repetition. We reveal that reasoning impasses trigger the loop onset, which subsequently persists as an inescapable cycle driven by a self-reinforcing V-shaped attention mechanism. Guided by these findings, we employ the Cumulative Sum (CUSUM) algorithm to capture these precursors for early loop prediction. Experiments across diverse LRMs validate its accuracy and elucidate the stability of long-chain reasoning.

papers.title: On the Connection between Game-Theoretic Feature Attributions and Counterfactual Explanations
papers.research_question: How do feature attribution based explanations and counterfactual explanations align with each other?
papers.core_contribution: Proves a theoretical equivalence between game-theoretic feature attributions (like SHAP) and counterfactual explanations under conditions such as maximal sparsity.
papers.conclusion: Connects feature attributions and counterfactual explanations, highlighting limitations of frequentist approaches and the role of sparsity.
papers.key_findings:
Under maximal sparsity, Bin-CF-SHAP and Norm-CF-Freq are equivalent.
Counterfactual frequency-based feature importance cannot differentiate between necessary, sufficient, and spurious features.
The equivalence extends to other game-theoretic solution concepts beyond Shapley values.
Empirical results show that explanations differ based on the operative changes.
Sparsity constraints are crucial for meaningful feature importance from counterfactuals.
papers.limitation: Maximal sparsity is a strong requirement for equivalence.
future_direction: Analyzing power indices like Deegan-Packel's and Holler-Packel's in relation to sparsity
Investigating how results reflect on causal feature importance and counterfactual explanations
papers.abstract: Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) has received widespread interest in recent years, and two of the most popular types of explanations are feature attributions, and counterfactual explanations. These classes of approaches have been largely studied independently and the few attempts at reconciling them have been primarily empirical. This work establishes a clear theoretical connection between game-theoretic feature attributions, focusing on but not limited to SHAP, and counterfactuals explanations. After motivating operative changes to Shapley values based feature attributions and counterfactual explanations, we prove that, under conditions, they are in fact equivalent. We then extend the equivalency result to game-theoretic solution concepts beyond Shapley values. Moreover, through the analysis of the conditions of such equivalence, we shed light on the limitations of naively using counterfactual explanations to provide feature importances. Experiments on three datasets quantitatively show the difference in explanations at every stage of the connection between the two approaches and corroborate the theoretical findings.

papers.title: ECINN: Efficient Counterfactuals from Invertible Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can counterfactual examples for image classification be generated efficiently using invertible neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: ECINN is an efficient method for generating counterfactual examples using invertible neural networks, requiring only a forward and inverse pass, with a closed-form correction in the latent space.
papers.conclusion: ECINN efficiently generates counterfactual examples that are realistic, change only class-dependent features, and provides both tipping-point and convincing counterfactuals, with ECINNh producing high-quality heatmaps for INNs.
papers.key_findings:
ECINN changes class-dependent features while leaving class-independent features largely untouched.
ECINN generates realistic counterfactual examples for digits and faces.
ECINNh produces heatmaps that are more coherent and meaningful than established methods like Integrated Gradients and DeepLift on INNs.
The method is efficient, requiring only two model evaluations per counterfactual.
The quality of counterfactuals depends on the trade-off between classification and generative performance controlled by the β parameter in IB-INN.
papers.limitation:
Some counterfactual examples on CelebA-HQ look unrealistic, with difficulty in opening and closing mouths, and small artifacts.
The method's performance may be limited by model size and resolution, as using larger models could improve quality.
papers.abstract: Counterfactual examples identify how inputs can be altered to change the predicted class of a classifier, thus opening up the black-box nature of, e.g., deep neural networks. We propose a method, ECINN, that utilizes the generative capacities of invertible neural networks for image classification to generate counterfactual examples efficiently. In contrast to competing methods that sometimes need a thousand evaluations or more of the classifier, ECINN has a closed-form expression and generates a counterfactual in the time of only two evaluations. Arguably, the main challenge of generating counterfactual examples is to alter only input features that affect the predicted outcome, i.e., class-dependent features. Our experiments demonstrate how ECINN alters class-dependent image regions to change the perceptual and predicted class of the counterfactuals. Additionally, we extend ECINN to also produce heatmaps (ECINNh) for easy inspection of, e.g., pairwise class-dependent changes in the generated counterfactual examples. Experimentally, we find that ECINNh outperforms established methods that generate heatmap-based explanations.

papers.title: Can LLMs Predict Their Own Failures? Self-Awareness via Internal Circuits
papers.research_question: Can LLMs predict their own failures by inspecting internal states during inference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Gnosis, a lightweight self-awareness mechanism that enables frozen LLMs to perform intrinsic self-verification by decoding signals from hidden states and attention patterns with negligible inference overhead.
papers.conclusion: Gnosis provides a highly efficient framework for self-evaluation and sibling modeling, enabling early error detection and compute-aware control, demonstrating that intrinsic self-verification is both scalable and cost-effective.
papers.key_findings:
Gnosis consistently outperforms strong internal baselines and large external judges (e.g., 8B reward models, Gemini 2.5 Pro) in accuracy and calibration across math reasoning, QA, and academic knowledge benchmarks.
Gnosis generalizes zero-shot to partial generations, enabling early detection of failing trajectories and compute-aware control.
A Gnosis head trained on a small backbone transfers effectively to judge larger sibling models without fine-tuning.
Gnosis adds only ~5M parameters and operates with negligible inference cost, independent of sequence length.
Results show that reliable correctness cues are intrinsic to the generation process and can be extracted efficiently without external supervision.
papers.limitation: Gnosis is designed as a self-awareness mechanism rather than a general-purpose reward model; it transfers robustly to siblings but is not capable of acting as a general reward model.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) generate fluent and complex outputs but often fail to recognize their own mistakes and hallucinations. Existing approaches typically rely on external judges, multi-sample consistency, or text-based self-critique, which incur additional compute or correlate weakly with true correctness. We ask: can LLMs predict their own failures by inspecting internal states during inference? We introduce Gnosis, a lightweight self-awareness mechanism that enables frozen LLMs to perform intrinsic self-verification by decoding signals from hidden states and attention patterns. Gnosis passively observes internal traces, compresses them into fixed-budget descriptors, and predicts correctness with negligible inference cost, adding only ~5M parameters and operating independently of sequence length. Across math reasoning, open-domain question answering, and academic knowledge benchmarks, and over frozen backbones ranging from 1.7B to 20B parameters, Gnosis consistently outperforms strong internal baselines and large external judges in both accuracy and calibration. Moreover, it generalizes zero-shot to partial generations, enabling early detection of failing trajectories and compute-aware control. These results show that reliable correctness cues are intrinsic to generation process and can be extracted efficiently without external supervision.

papers.title: Towards Best Practices of Activation Patching in Language Models: Metrics and Methods
papers.research_question: How do different methodological choices in activation patching, such as corruption methods and evaluation metrics, affect localization and circuit discovery results in language models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper systematically evaluates hyperparameters in activation patching for language models, finding that choices of corruption methods and metrics significantly affect interpretability results, and provides best practice recommendations.
papers.conclusion: The paper recommends using symmetric token replacement (STR) for in-distribution corruption and logit difference as the evaluation metric for activation patching, highlighting the sensitivity of interpretability results to methodological details.
papers.key_findings:
GN and STR corruption methods lead to inconsistent localization and circuit discovery outcomes.
Probability metric can overlook negative model components that hurt performance, while logit difference is capable of detecting them.
Sliding window patching produces more pronounced localization than summing single-layer patching effects, potentially amplifying weak signals.
GN corruption may put the model off-distribution, breaking internal mechanisms and leading to unreliable interpretability results.
Logit difference is recommended over probability for fine-grained control and detecting negative modules.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability seeks to understand the internal mechanisms of machine learning models, where localization -- identifying the important model components -- is a key step. Activation patching, also known as causal tracing or interchange intervention, is a standard technique for this task (Vig et al., 2020), but the literature contains many variants with little consensus on the choice of hyperparameters or methodology. In this work, we systematically examine the impact of methodological details in activation patching, including evaluation metrics and corruption methods. In several settings of localization and circuit discovery in language models, we find that varying these hyperparameters could lead to disparate interpretability results. Backed by empirical observations, we give conceptual arguments for why certain metrics or methods may be preferred. Finally, we provide recommendations for the best practices of activation patching going forwards.

papers.title: A Survey on Latent Reasoning
papers.research_question: This paper investigates latent reasoning as an alternative to explicit chain-of-thought in large language models, exploring its methods, benefits, and future directions.
papers.core_contribution: This survey provides a comprehensive overview of latent reasoning, categorizing methods into activation-based and hidden state-based approaches, and discusses future directions for research at the frontier of LLM cognition.
papers.conclusion: The survey unifies perspectives on latent reasoning and charts future directions for research at the frontier of LLM cognition.
papers.key_findings:
Latent reasoning performs multi-step inference in continuous hidden states, offering higher bandwidth than explicit chain-of-thought.
Activation-based methods create deeper computational graphs by iteratively processing information through the same layers.
Hidden-state-based methods expand temporal capacity by evolving hidden states over sequences.
Diffusion models enable infinite-depth reasoning through bidirectional context and iterative refinement.
Layer specialization theory suggests different layers play distinct roles in latent reasoning, analogous to steps in explicit CoT.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive reasoning capabilities, especially when guided by explicit chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning that verbalizes intermediate steps. While CoT improves both interpretability and accuracy, its dependence on natural language reasoning limits the model's expressive bandwidth. Latent reasoning tackles this bottleneck by performing multi-step inference entirely in the model's continuous hidden state, eliminating token-level supervision. To advance latent reasoning research, this survey provides a comprehensive overview of the emerging field of latent reasoning. We begin by examining the foundational role of neural network layers as the computational substrate for reasoning, highlighting how hierarchical representations support complex transformations. Next, we explore diverse latent reasoning methodologies, including activation-based recurrence, hidden state propagation, and fine-tuning strategies that compress or internalize explicit reasoning traces. Finally, we discuss advanced paradigms such as infinite-depth latent reasoning via masked diffusion models, which enable globally consistent and reversible reasoning processes. By unifying these perspectives, we aim to clarify the conceptual landscape of latent reasoning and chart future directions for research at the frontier of LLM cognition. An associated GitHub repository collecting the latest papers and repos is available at: https://github.com/multimodal-art-projection/LatentCoT-Horizon/.

papers.title: Can LLMs Lie? Investigation beyond Hallucination
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether LLMs can intentionally lie (as opposed to unintentionally hallucinate), and how to understand and control lying behavior using mechanistic interpretability.
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers the neural mechanisms of lying in LLMs using mechanistic interpretability, and introduces steering vectors to control lying behavior, showing a trade-off between honesty and task performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that lying in LLMs can be understood and controlled via mechanistic interpretability, and highlights the trade-offs between honesty and task success in real-world scenarios.
papers.key_findings:
Lying ability in LLMs improves with model size and reasoning capabilities.
LLMs use dummy tokens as a computational scratchpad for lying, with specific attention heads and MLP modules involved.
Lying circuits are sparse and can be ablated to reduce deception without broadly degrading model utility.
Different types of lies (white vs. malicious, commission vs. omission) are linearly separable in activation space and controllable via distinct steering directions.
Steering vectors can increase honesty in multi-turn conversational settings, establishing a Pareto frontier between honesty and goal completion.
papers.limitation:
Analysis confined to a few model families and sizes.
Steering vectors derived from a limited set of contrastive prompts.
Multi-turn conversational setting is simplified.
Honesty steering vectors applied in the negative direction may lead to mass production of false information.
future_direction: Scaling the approach to larger models and more complex scenarios.
Investigating the transferability of steering vectors across domains.
Developing more robust safeguards against deceptive AI.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities across a variety of tasks, but their increasing autonomy in real-world applications raises concerns about their trustworthiness. While hallucinations-unintentional falsehoods-have been widely studied, the phenomenon of lying, where an LLM knowingly generates falsehoods to achieve an ulterior objective, remains underexplored. In this work, we systematically investigate the lying behavior of LLMs, differentiating it from hallucinations and testing it in practical scenarios. Through mechanistic interpretability techniques, we uncover the neural mechanisms underlying deception, employing logit lens analysis, causal interventions, and contrastive activation steering to identify and control deceptive behavior. We study real-world lying scenarios and introduce behavioral steering vectors that enable fine-grained manipulation of lying tendencies. Further, we explore the trade-offs between lying and end-task performance, establishing a Pareto frontier where dishonesty can enhance goal optimization. Our findings contribute to the broader discourse on AI ethics, shedding light on the risks and potential safeguards for deploying LLMs in high-stakes environments. Code and more illustrations are available at https://llm-liar.github.io/

papers.title: I Have Covered All the Bases Here: Interpreting Reasoning Features in Large Language Models via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How are reasoning capabilities internally encoded within large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ReasonScore, an automatic metric to identify reasoning features in LLMs using sparse autoencoders, and provides causal evidence that amplifying these features improves reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: This work provides a first step towards a mechanistic understanding of reasoning in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
ReasonScore identifies SAE features corresponding to uncertainty, exploration, and reflection.
Steering these features improves performance on reasoning benchmarks and leads to longer reasoning traces.
These reasoning features are present only in models with reasoning capabilities, as shown by model diffing.
papers.abstract: Recent LLMs like DeepSeek-R1 have demonstrated state-of-the-art performance by integrating deep thinking and complex reasoning during generation. However, the internal mechanisms behind these reasoning processes remain unexplored. We observe reasoning LLMs consistently use vocabulary associated with human reasoning processes. We hypothesize these words correspond to specific reasoning moments within the models' internal mechanisms. To test this hypothesis, we employ Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), a technique for sparse decomposition of neural network activations into human-interpretable features. We introduce ReasonScore, an automatic metric to identify active SAE features during these reasoning moments. We perform manual and automatic interpretation of the features detected by our metric, and find those with activation patterns matching uncertainty, exploratory thinking, and reflection. Through steering experiments, we demonstrate that amplifying these features increases performance on reasoning-intensive benchmarks (+2.2%) while producing longer reasoning traces (+20.5%). Using the model diffing technique, we provide evidence that these features are present only in models with reasoning capabilities. Our work provides the first step towards a mechanistic understanding of reasoning in LLMs. Code available at https://github.com/AIRI-Institute/SAE-Reasoning

papers.title: Grokked Transformers are Implicit Reasoners: A Mechanistic Journey to the Edge of Generalization
papers.research_question: Can transformers learn implicit reasoning over parametric knowledge, and how does grokking enable this? What are the differences in systematic generalization between composition and comparison tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers can learn implicit reasoning over parametric knowledge through grokking, but systematic generalization varies: composition fails out-of-distribution while comparison succeeds. Mechanistic analysis reveals the formation of generalizing circuits and explains the differences, guiding data and training setups and suggesting architectural improvements.
papers.conclusion: Transformers are capable of learning implicit reasoning through grokking, but the level of systematic generalization depends on the task and the circuit configuration. The findings guide data and training setups and suggest improvements to the transformer architecture for better cross-layer memory sharing.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers can learn implicit reasoning only through grokking (extended training far beyond overfitting).
The speed of grokking correlates with the ratio of inferred to atomic facts (data distribution), not the absolute training data size.
For composition, transformers fail to generalize systematically to out-of-distribution examples, while for comparison, they succeed.
Mechanistic analysis reveals distinct generalizing circuits: for composition, a sequential circuit that stores atomic facts in separate layers; for comparison, a parallel circuit that stores atomic facts in the same layer.
In a complex reasoning task with a large search space, a fully grokked transformer achieves near-perfect accuracy, while state-of-the-art LLMs with non-parametric memory (GPT-4-Turbo, Gemini-1.5-Pro) fail regardless of prompting or retrieval augmentation.
papers.limitation:
The task formulation (induction and application of inference rules from atomic and inferred facts) may not apply to the full spectrum of reasoning types.
The study is limited to synthetic tasks and may not fully capture real-world reasoning complexities.
future_direction: Developing cross-layer memory-sharing mechanisms for transformers (e.g., memory-augmentation, explicit recurrence) to improve systematic generalization.
Investigating the tradeoff between parametric and non-parametric memory in language models.
Understanding the role of verbalizations (e.g., chain-of-thought) in teaching models to reason implicitly.
papers.abstract: We study whether transformers can learn to implicitly reason over parametric knowledge, a skill that even the most capable language models struggle with. Focusing on two representative reasoning types, composition and comparison, we consistently find that transformers can learn implicit reasoning, but only through grokking, i.e., extended training far beyond overfitting. The levels of generalization also vary across reasoning types: when faced with out-of-distribution examples, transformers fail to systematically generalize for composition but succeed for comparison. We delve into the model's internals throughout training, conducting analytical experiments that reveal: 1) the mechanism behind grokking, such as the formation of the generalizing circuit and its relation to the relative efficiency of generalizing and memorizing circuits, and 2) the connection between systematicity and the configuration of the generalizing circuit. Our findings guide data and training setup to better induce implicit reasoning and suggest potential improvements to the transformer architecture, such as encouraging cross-layer knowledge sharing. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for a challenging reasoning task with a large search space, GPT-4-Turbo and Gemini-1.5-Pro based on non-parametric memory fail badly regardless of prompting styles or retrieval augmentation, while a fully grokked transformer can achieve near-perfect accuracy, showcasing the power of parametric memory for complex reasoning.

papers.title: Cognitive Foundations for Reasoning and Their Manifestation in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do cognitive elements of reasoning manifest in LLMs, and how do they differ from human reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a taxonomy of 28 cognitive elements for reasoning and conducts a large-scale empirical analysis of human and LLM reasoning traces, revealing that LLMs underutilize cognitive elements correlated with success and that test-time reasoning guidance can improve performance.
papers.conclusion: The taxonomy provides a shared vocabulary for diagnosing reasoning failures and enables principled development of models that reason through robust cognitive mechanisms, while models possess latent capabilities that can be elicited with structural guidance.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs underutilize cognitive elements that are correlated with success, especially on ill-structured problems.
Humans use more abstraction and conceptual processing, while LLMs rely on surface-level enumeration.
Test-time reasoning guidance that scaffolds successful cognitive structures improves performance by up to 66.7% on complex problems.
The research community focuses on easily quantifiable cognitive elements (like sequential organization) and neglects meta-cognitive controls (like self-awareness).
Models possess behavioral repertoires associated with success but fail to deploy them spontaneously.
papers.limitation:
Human participants are educated adults; comparison with children might yield different insights.
Models are tested on a limited set of problem types.
future_direction: Using the taxonomy for training and evaluation of LLMs
Developing cognitive architectures based on the taxonomy
Extending the analysis to more problem types and models
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) solve complex problems yet fail on simpler variants, suggesting they achieve correct outputs through mechanisms fundamentally different from human reasoning. To understand this gap, we synthesize cognitive science research into a taxonomy of 28 cognitive elements spanning reasoning invariants, meta-cognitive controls, representations for organizing reasoning & knowledge, and transformation operations. We introduce a fine-grained evaluation framework and conduct the first large-scale empirical analysis of 192K traces from 18 models across text, vision, and audio, complemented by 54 human think-aloud traces, which we make publicly available. We find that models under-utilize cognitive elements correlated with success, narrowing to rigid sequential processing on ill-structured problems where diverse representations and meta-cognitive monitoring are critical. Human traces show more abstraction and conceptual processing, while models default to surface-level enumeration. Meta-analysis of 1.6K LLM reasoning papers reveals the research community concentrates on easily quantifiable elements (sequential organization: 55%, decomposition: 60%) but neglecting meta-cognitive controls (self-awareness: 16%) that correlate with success. Models possess behavioral repertoires associated with success but fail to deploy them spontaneously. Leveraging these patterns, we develop test-time reasoning guidance that automatically scaffold successful structures, improving performance by up to 66.7% on complex problems. By establishing a shared vocabulary between cognitive science and LLM research, our framework enables systematic diagnosis of reasoning failures and principled development of models that reason through robust cognitive mechanisms rather than spurious shortcuts, while providing tools to test theories of human cognition at scale.

papers.title: Mechanistic Indicators of Understanding in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) possess genuine understanding, and if so, what forms does it take? The paper investigates this by synthesizing findings from mechanistic interpretability within a philosophical framework.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a tiered framework (conceptual, state-of-the-world, principled understanding) for assessing understanding in LLMs and synthesizes mechanistic interpretability evidence to argue that LLMs can develop internal organizations that underwrite understanding-like unification, though these mechanisms diverge from human cognition.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic interpretability reveals internal organizations in LLMs that can underwrite understanding-like unification across conceptual, factual, and principled tiers, but these mechanisms diverge from human cognition in their parallel exploitation of heterogeneous, task-specific pathways.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs develop internal 'features' (e.g., a 'Golden Gate Bridge' feature in Claude 3 Sonnet) that act as conceptual unifiers, connecting diverse manifestations of entities or properties.
The linear representation hypothesis is supported, with features encoded as directions in latent space, and superposition allows for efficient representation of many features.
Models like Othello-GPT develop internal 'world models' (e.g., of the board state) that are causally involved in task performance, as shown via probing and intervention techniques.
The phenomenon of 'grokking' demonstrates a shift from memorization to discovering compact, generalizable circuits (e.g., for modular arithmetic), indicative of principled understanding.
Higher-tier understanding mechanisms coexist with lower-tier heuristics (e.g., memorization, n-gram statistics) within LLMs, impacting their epistemic trustworthiness.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are often portrayed as merely imitating linguistic patterns without genuine understanding. We argue that recent findings in mechanistic interpretability (MI), the emerging field probing the inner workings of LLMs, render this picture increasingly untenable--but only once those findings are integrated within a theoretical account of understanding. We propose a tiered framework for thinking about understanding in LLMs and use it to synthesize the most relevant findings to date. The framework distinguishes three hierarchical varieties of understanding, each tied to a corresponding level of computational organization: conceptual understanding emerges when a model forms "features" as directions in latent space, learning connections between diverse manifestations of a single entity or property; state-of-the-world understanding emerges when a model learns contingent factual connections between features and dynamically tracks changes in the world; principled understanding emerges when a model ceases to rely on memorized facts and discovers a compact "circuit" connecting these facts. Across these tiers, MI uncovers internal organizations that can underwrite understanding-like unification. However, these also diverge from human cognition in their parallel exploitation of heterogeneous mechanisms. Fusing philosophical theory with mechanistic evidence thus allows us to transcend binary debates over whether AI understands, paving the way for a comparative, mechanistically grounded epistemology that explores how AI understanding aligns with--and diverges from--our own.

papers.title: Emergent Symbolic Mechanisms Support Abstract Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What internal mechanisms support abstract reasoning in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies an emergent three-stage symbolic architecture in LLMs that implements abstract reasoning via symbol abstraction heads, symbolic induction heads, and retrieval heads.
papers.conclusion: LLMs perform abstract reasoning via emergent symbolic mechanisms, suggesting a resolution to the debate between symbolic and neural network approaches.
papers.key_findings:
Symbol abstraction heads in early layers convert input tokens to abstract variables based on relations.
Symbolic induction heads in intermediate layers perform sequence induction over abstract variables.
Retrieval heads in later layers retrieve the token associated with the predicted abstract variable.
These mechanisms are robust across multiple abstract reasoning tasks and model families.
Representations in these heads encode abstract variables invariant to specific tokens, and better representation correlates with correct performance.
papers.abstract: Many recent studies have found evidence for emergent reasoning capabilities in large language models (LLMs), but debate persists concerning the robustness of these capabilities, and the extent to which they depend on structured reasoning mechanisms. To shed light on these issues, we study the internal mechanisms that support abstract reasoning in LLMs. We identify an emergent symbolic architecture that implements abstract reasoning via a series of three computations. In early layers, symbol abstraction heads convert input tokens to abstract variables based on the relations between those tokens. In intermediate layers, symbolic induction heads perform sequence induction over these abstract variables. Finally, in later layers, retrieval heads predict the next token by retrieving the value associated with the predicted abstract variable. These results point toward a resolution of the longstanding debate between symbolic and neural network approaches, suggesting that emergent reasoning in neural networks depends on the emergence of symbolic mechanisms.

papers.title: Identifying Semantic Induction Heads to Understand In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether attention heads in transformers encode semantic relationships (syntactic dependencies and knowledge graph relations) and how the formation of such semantic induction heads correlates with the emergence of in-context learning abilities.
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers semantic induction heads in transformers that encode semantic relationships and shows their emergence correlates with the development of in-context learning abilities.
papers.conclusion: The study of semantic induction heads advances understanding of attention head operations and provides insights into the in-context learning of LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads in transformers encode syntactic dependencies (subj, obj, mod) and semantic relationships from knowledge graphs.
The model's ability to understand dependencies is reflected in attention heads, with some heads specializing in specific relations.
In-context learning emerges progressively in three levels: loss reduction, format compliance, and pattern discovery.
The formation of semantic induction heads coincides with the emergence of pattern discovery in ICL.
Semantic induction heads are crucial for the model's ability to perform in-context learning.
papers.abstract: Although large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance, the lack of transparency in their inference logic raises concerns about their trustworthiness. To gain a better understanding of LLMs, we conduct a detailed analysis of the operations of attention heads and aim to better understand the in-context learning of LLMs. Specifically, we investigate whether attention heads encode two types of relationships between tokens present in natural languages: the syntactic dependency parsed from sentences and the relation within knowledge graphs. We find that certain attention heads exhibit a pattern where, when attending to head tokens, they recall tail tokens and increase the output logits of those tail tokens. More crucially, the formulation of such semantic induction heads has a close correlation with the emergence of the in-context learning ability of language models. The study of semantic attention heads advances our understanding of the intricate operations of attention heads in transformers, and further provides new insights into the in-context learning of LLMs.

papers.title: Mechanistic understanding and validation of large AI models with SemanticLens
papers.research_question: How can we achieve automated explanation and validation of model components at scale to understand their inner knowledge and ensure alignment with human expectations?
papers.core_contribution: SemanticLens is a universal explanation method that embeds neural network components into the semantic space of a foundation model, enabling scalable search, description, comparison, and auditing of learned concepts for component-level understanding and validation.
papers.conclusion: By enabling component-level understanding and validation, SemanticLens helps mitigate the opacity of AI models, facilitating more reliable deployment in critical applications.
papers.key_findings:
SemanticLens enables text-based search to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, such as biases or data artefacts, in models like ResNet50v2.
It can describe and structure the internal knowledge of models through semantic embeddings, revealing clusters of concepts like animals and vehicles.
The method allows auditing of concept alignment with expected reasoning, detecting spurious correlations and measuring reliance on valid vs. spurious concepts.
In medical image analysis, SemanticLens identifies spurious components (e.g., scale bars, band-aids) and enables model correction via pruning or retraining, improving robustness.
It introduces interpretability measures (clarity, polysemanticity, redundancy) that correlate with human perception and vary across architectures and training regimes.
papers.limitation: Concepts may be distributed across several components, and the neural basis may not comprehensively capture all relevant concepts.
papers.abstract: Abstract Unlike human-engineered systems, such as aeroplanes, for which the role and dependencies of each component are well understood, the inner workings of artificial intelligence models remain largely opaque, which hinders verifiability and undermines trust. Current approaches to neural network interpretability, including input attribution methods, probe-based analysis and activation visualization techniques, typically provide limited insights about the role of individual components or require extensive manual interpretation that cannot scale with model complexity. This paper introduces SemanticLens, a universal explanation method for neural networks that maps hidden knowledge encoded by components (for example, individual neurons) into the semantically structured, multimodal space of a foundation model such as CLIP. In this space, unique operations become possible, including (1) textual searches to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, (2) systematic analysis and comparison of model representations, (3) automated labelling of neurons and explanation of their functional roles, and (4) audits to validate decision-making against requirements. Fully scalable and operating without human input, SemanticLens is shown to be effective for debugging and validation, summarizing model knowledge, aligning reasoning with expectations (for example, adherence to the ABCDE rule in melanoma classification) and detecting components tied to spurious correlations and their associated training data. By enabling component-level understanding and validation, the proposed approach helps mitigate the opacity that limits confidence in artificial intelligence systems compared to traditional engineered systems, enabling more reliable deployment in critical applications.

papers.title: Semantics-Adaptive Activation Intervention for LLMs via Dynamic Steering Vectors
papers.research_question: How can activation intervention methods be made adaptive to the semantic context of inputs, overcoming the limitation of fixed steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SADI, a dynamic activation intervention method that constructs a steering vector tailored to each input's semantic context, improving task performance without training and generalizing across various LLMs and tasks.
papers.conclusion: SADI advances activation engineering by providing a dynamic and adaptive intervention method that significantly improves model performance across diverse tasks and models without requiring training.
papers.key_findings:
SADI outperforms fixed steering baseline methods (ITI, CAA) by substantial margins across multiple-choice and open-ended generation tasks.
SADI is effective across different model backbones (LLAMA2, BLOOMZ, MISTRAL, FALCON) and model sizes (560M to 7B).
SADI works in few-shot and multilingual settings, demonstrating broad generalizability.
SADI requires only a small number of contrastive pairs (e.g., 150) and no training, making it cost-effective.
Interventions targeting attention heads (SADI-HEAD) consistently yield significant performance improvements across tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable performance across many tasks, yet aligning them with desired behaviors remains challenging. Activation intervention has emerged as an effective and economical method to modify the behavior of LLMs. Despite considerable interest in this area, current intervention methods exclusively employ a fixed steering vector to modify model activations, lacking adaptability to diverse input semantics. To address this limitation, we propose Semantics-Adaptive Dynamic Intervention (SADI), a novel method that constructs a dynamic steering vector to intervene model activations at inference time. More specifically, SADI utilizes activation differences in contrastive pairs to precisely identify critical elements of an LLM (i.e., attention heads, hidden states, and neurons) for targeted intervention. During inference, SADI dynamically steers model behavior by scaling element-wise activations based on the directions of input semantics. Experimental results show that SADI outperforms established baselines by substantial margins, improving task performance without training. SADI's cost-effectiveness and generalizability across various LLM backbones and tasks highlight its potential as a versatile alignment technique.

papers.title: Diagnosing Knowledge Conflict in Multimodal Long-Chain Reasoning
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) in long chain-of-thought reasoning often fail when different knowledge sources provide conflicting signals. We formalize these failures under a unified notion of knowledge conflict, distinguishing input-level objective conflict from process-level effective conflict. Through probing internal representations, we reveal that: (I) Linear Separability: different conflict types are explicitly encoded as linearly separable features rather than entangled; (II) Depth Localization: conflict signals concentrate in mid-to-late layers, indicating a distinct processing stage for conflict encoding; (III) Hierarchical Consistency: aggregating noisy token-level signals along trajectories robustly recovers input-level conflict types; and (IV) Directional Asymmetry: reinforcing the model's implicit source preference under conflict is far easier than enforcing the opposite source. Our findings provide a mechanism-level view of multimodal reasoning under knowledge conflict and enable principled diagnosis and control of long-CoT failures.

papers.title: Function Induction and Task Generalization: An Interpretability Study with Off-by-One Addition
papers.research_question: What mechanisms inside large language models drive task-level generalization via in-context learning, specifically through the lens of off-by-one addition?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a 'function induction' mechanism in transformer language models that explains how they generalize from seen to unseen tasks via in-context learning, particularly for multi-step tasks like off-by-one addition.
papers.conclusion: The findings offer deeper insights into how reusable and composable structures within language models enable task-level generalization.
papers.key_findings:
The model's generalization from standard addition to off-by-one addition is explained by a circuit resembling induction heads but operating at a function level, termed 'function induction'.
The induction of the +1 function is governed by multiple attention heads (FI heads) in parallel, each emitting a distinct piece of the function.
The same function induction mechanism is reused in a broader range of tasks, including shifted multiple-choice QA, Caesar cipher, and base-8 addition.
The circuit involves three groups of attention heads: consolidation heads (Group 1), function induction heads (Group 2), and previous token heads (Group 3).
The mechanism is found across multiple models (Gemma-2, Mistral, Llama-2, Llama-3), though with variations.
papers.limitation: The exact role of consolidation heads and why they emerge remains limited, relating to the broader challenge of interpreting 'negative' behavior in language models.
future_direction: Finer-grained interpretation of consolidation heads and their role.
Further investigation into the differences between FI heads and FV heads (function vector heads).
Training toy models to perform off-by-one addition and isolating the circuit requires separate study.
papers.abstract: Large language models demonstrate the intriguing ability to perform unseen tasks via in-context learning. However, it remains unclear what mechanisms inside the model drive such task-level generalization. In this work, we approach this question through the lens of off-by-one addition (i.e., 1+1=3, 2+2=5, 3+3=?), a two-step, counterfactual task with an unexpected +1 function as a second step. Leveraging circuit-style interpretability techniques such as path patching, we analyze the models' internal computations behind their performance and present three key findings. First, we uncover a function induction mechanism that explains the model's generalization from standard addition to off-by-one addition. This mechanism resembles the structure of the induction head mechanism found in prior work and elevates it to a higher level of abstraction. Second, we show that the induction of the +1 function is governed by multiple attention heads in parallel, each of which emits a distinct piece of the +1 function. Finally, we find that this function induction mechanism is reused in a broader range of tasks, including synthetic tasks such as shifted multiple-choice QA and algorithmic tasks such as base-8 addition. Overall, our findings offer deeper insights into how reusable and composable structures within language models enable task-level generalization.

papers.title: Decoding In-Context Learning: Neuroscience-inspired Analysis of Representations in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do LLM embeddings and attention representations change following in-context learning, and how do these changes mediate improvement in behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a neuroscience-inspired framework using Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) and Attention Ratio Analysis (ARA) to show that in-context learning improves task-critical representations and attention allocation, which correlate with behavioral gains.
papers.conclusion: ICL improves task-critical representations and attention allocation to relevant content in the prompt, and these representational changes are correlated with behavioral gains.
papers.key_findings:
ICL leads to changes in prompt embedding similarity matrices to better encode task-critical information, which in turn improves behavior.
ICL increases the decodability of task-critical information (e.g., line slope) from embeddings via probing classifiers.
ICL shifts attention to relevant content in the prompt (increased attention ratio to informative parts), which correlates with behavioral improvement.
These representational changes are consistent across multiple layers (except the first) in both Llama-2 and Vicuna models.
The proposed methods (RSA and ARA) provide scalable tools for analyzing latent representations in large language models.
future_direction: Study the effects of ICL on improving planning behavior in LLMs by analyzing latent representations before and after ICL in planning tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable performance improvement through in-context learning (ICL) by leveraging task-specific examples in the input. However, the mechanisms behind this improvement remain elusive. In this work, we investigate how LLM embeddings and attention representations change following in-context-learning, and how these changes mediate improvement in behavior. We employ neuroscience-inspired techniques such as representational similarity analysis (RSA) and propose novel methods for parameterized probing and measuring ratio of attention to relevant vs. irrelevant information in Llama-2 70B and Vicuna 13B. We designed two tasks with a priori relationships among their conditions: linear regression and reading comprehension. We formed hypotheses about expected similarities in task representations and measured hypothesis alignment of LLM representations before and after ICL as well as changes in attention. Our analyses revealed a meaningful correlation between improvements in behavior after ICL and changes in both embeddings and attention weights across LLM layers. This empirical framework empowers a nuanced understanding of how latent representations shape LLM behavior, offering valuable tools and insights for future research and practical applications.

papers.title: Alignment Via Interpretability: Layerwise Counterfactuals To Detect Maladaptive Llm Behaviors
papers.research_question: How can layerwise counterfactual interventions on internal representations detect maladaptive behaviors in large language models that are not reliably exposed through prompt-based evaluation alone?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a layerwise counterfactual interpretability framework that detects maladaptive behaviors in LLMs by performing causal interventions on internal representations, demonstrating that intermediate layers encode decision-critical features for alignment.
papers.conclusion: The layerwise counterfactual framework enables proactive detection of alignment risks by revealing internal representations causally linked to maladaptive behaviors, positioning interpretability as a diagnostic tool for safety.
papers.key_findings:
Intermediate layers consistently show the highest causal influence on alignment behavior, often flipping responses between refusal and compliance.
Counterfactual interventions can induce maladaptive behaviors even when baseline outputs appear aligned, revealing latent misalignment.
Layerwise sensitivity patterns are stable across different model checkpoints and random seeds.
Early layers encode surface linguistic features with minimal impact on alignment decisions.
Late layers modulate stylistic aspects of responses rather than core decision outcomes.
papers.limitation:
Counterfactual interventions establish causal influence but do not directly reveal how misalignment features are learned during training.
The analysis focuses on decoder-only transformer architectures, and findings may not fully generalize to other model families or multimodal systems.
Behavioral evaluation metrics, though carefully designed, cannot exhaustively capture all forms of maladaptive behavior.
Interpretability methods may miss distributed or nonlinear representations that do not localize cleanly within individual layers.
future_direction: Extending the framework to larger models, multimodal architectures, and training time interventions.
Integrating counterfactual diagnostics into alignment training loops.
Formalizing metrics for internal alignment robustness.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Large language model alignment remains fragile under distribution shift, jailbreak prompts, and latent goal misgeneralization, motivating the need for diagnostic tools that move beyond surface level behavior to internal representations. This paper investigates alignment via interpretability by introducing a layerwise counterfactual analysis framework that probes how targeted interventions on hidden states alter downstream model behavior. Using publicly available transformer based language models and open interpretability tooling, we perform controlled counterfactual substitutions and activation patching across layers to detect maladaptive behaviors that are not reliably exposed through prompt based evaluation alone. Our analysis demonstrates that specific intermediate layers encode decision critical features whose perturbation consistently induces alignment failures such as reward hacking tendencies, deceptive compliance, and instruction misgeneralization, even when input level behavior appears aligned. We further show that these internal signatures are stable across random seeds and model checkpoints, enabling reproducible detection of misalignment risks prior to deployment. The findings support the thesis that interpretability driven diagnostics can serve as an early warning mechanism for alignment failures and provide a principled foundation for integrating internal model transparency into safety evaluation pipelines.

papers.title: On the Paradox of Learning to Reason from Data
papers.research_question: Can a BERT model be trained end-to-end to solve logical reasoning problems presented in natural language?
papers.core_contribution: BERT can achieve near-perfect accuracy on in-distribution logical reasoning problems but fails to generalize to other distributions in the same problem space because it learns statistical features instead of the reasoning function.
papers.conclusion: Learning to reason from data is difficult because models tend to learn statistical features instead of the reasoning function.
papers.key_findings:
BERT attains near-perfect accuracy on in-distribution test examples in the SimpleLogic problem space.
BERT fails to generalize to examples sampled from the same problem space but with a different distribution (e.g., from RP to LP).
Statistical features (like number of rules) inherently exist in logical reasoning problems and are correlated with labels.
BERT uses these statistical features to make predictions, which explains the generalization failure.
It is computationally expensive to jointly remove multiple statistical features from the training data.
papers.abstract: Logical reasoning is needed in a wide range of NLP tasks. Can a BERT model be trained end-to-end to solve logical reasoning problems presented in natural language? We attempt to answer this question in a confined problem space where there exists a set of parameters that perfectly simulates logical reasoning. We make observations that seem to contradict each other: BERT attains near-perfect accuracy on in-distribution test examples while failing to generalize to other data distributions over the exact same problem space. Our study provides an explanation for this paradox: instead of learning to emulate the correct reasoning function, BERT has in fact learned statistical features that inherently exist in logical reasoning problems. We also show that it is infeasible to jointly remove statistical features from data, illustrating the difficulty of learning to reason in general. Our result naturally extends to other neural models and unveils the fundamental difference between learning to reason and learning to achieve high performance on NLP benchmarks using statistical features.

papers.title: Pixels Versus Priors: Controlling Knowledge Priors in Vision-Language Models through Visual Counterfacts
papers.research_question: How do multimodal large language models (MLLMs) balance memorized world knowledge priors and visual input when they conflict?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Visual CounterFact, a dataset of visual counterfactuals, and PvP steering vectors, a method to control whether MLLMs rely on visual input or memorized world knowledge.
papers.conclusion: Provides a new framework for interpreting and controlling MLLMs, advancing the ability to understand and control the interaction between memory and perception.
papers.key_findings:
MLLMs often ignore world knowledge when shown counterfactual images, favoring perceptual input even when prompted for general facts.
Model predictions shift from memorized priors to visual evidence in mid-to-late layers, revealing a competition between modalities.
PvP steering vectors can successfully shift model predictions from world knowledge to counterfactual answers with high success rates (e.g., 99.3% for color).
Steering vectors reshape internal attention mechanisms more effectively than prompt changes alone.
There is an asymmetry: steering from world knowledge to counterfactuals is easier than the reverse.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on three state-of-the-art models, which do not represent the full spectrum of multimodal architectures.
Steering models from visual perception back to world knowledge is more difficult than the reverse, suggesting an asymmetry.
future_direction: Expand analysis to a broader range of models to explore how architectural design impacts reliance on perception versus prior knowledge.
Further understand the asymmetry in how MLLMs prioritize in-context versus memorized information.
papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) perform well on tasks such as visual question answering, but it remains unclear whether their reasoning relies more on memorized world knowledge or on the visual information present in the input image. To investigate this, we introduce Visual CounterFact, a new dataset of visually-realistic counterfactuals that put world knowledge priors (e.g, red strawberry) into direct conflict with visual input (e.g, blue strawberry). Using Visual CounterFact, we show that model predictions initially reflect memorized priors, but shift toward visual evidence in mid-to-late layers. This dynamic reveals a competition between the two modalities, with visual input ultimately overriding priors during evaluation. To control this behavior, we propose Pixels Versus Priors (PvP) steering vectors, a mechanism for controlling model outputs toward either world knowledge or visual input through activation-level interventions. On average, PvP successfully shifts 99.3% of color and 80.8% of size predictions from priors to counterfactuals. Together, these findings offer new tools for interpreting and controlling factual behavior in multimodal models.

papers.title: From Chains to DAGs: Probing the Graph Structure of Reasoning in LLMs
papers.research_question: Does the internal representation of LLMs encode graph-structured reasoning (as directed acyclic graphs) beyond linear chains, and where does this structure emerge across layers?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Reasoning DAG Probing, a framework to test whether LLM hidden states linearly encode reasoning DAG structure, and finds that such structure is meaningfully encoded, peaking in intermediate layers, and varies with node depth, edge span, and model scale.
papers.conclusion: LLM reasoning is not purely sequential, but exhibits measurable internal graph structure.
papers.key_findings:
DAG structure is meaningfully encoded in LLM representations.
Recoverability of DAG structure peaks in intermediate layers.
Recovery varies systematically by node depth, edge span, and model scale.
The framework enables nontrivial recovery of dependency graphs.
Larger models achieve higher recoverability, and reasoning-oriented training recipes provide modest gains.
papers.limitation:
The study focuses on frozen pretrained models; it remains open whether fine-tuning or reinforcement learning alters the internal geometry of reasoning.
The probing approach assumes that reasoning DAG structure is linearly accessible in hidden states; nonlinear or distributed encodings may require more expressive probes.
The DAG formalization for GSM8K relies on GPT-5 mini, which may introduce noise or bias.
future_direction: Extend the framework to dynamic or cyclic reasoning.
Incorporate more expressive probes.
Investigate how training interventions affect internal reasoning structure.
papers.abstract: Recent progress in large language models has renewed interest in mechanistically characterizing how multi-step reasoning is represented and computed. While much prior work treats reasoning as a linear chain of steps, many reasoning problems are more naturally structured as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), where intermediate conclusions may depend on multiple premises, branch into parallel sub-derivations, and later merge or be reused. Understanding whether such graph-structured reasoning is reflected in model internals remains an open question. In this work, we introduce Reasoning DAG Probing, a framework that directly asks whether LLM hidden states encode the geometry of a reasoning DAG in a linearly accessible form, and where this structure emerges across layers. Within this framework, we associate each reasoning node with a textual realization and train lightweight probes to predict two graph-theoretic properties from hidden states: node depth and pairwise node distance. We use these probes to analyze the layerwise emergence of DAG structure and evaluate controls that disrupt reasoning-relevant structure while preserving superficial textual properties. Our results provide evidence that reasoning DAG geometry is meaningfully encoded in intermediate layers, with recoverability varying systematically by node depth and model scale, suggesting that LLM reasoning is not only sequential but exhibits measurable internal graph structure.

papers.title: The Vector Grounding Problem
papers.research_question: Can large language models (LLMs) have internal states and outputs that are referentially grounded in the world, i.e., have intrinsic meaning, despite being trained only on text data without direct interaction with the world?
papers.core_contribution: Argues that large language models can achieve referential grounding (intrinsic meaning) through selection processes in training that endow internal states with representational functions, even without multimodality or embodiment.
papers.conclusion: LLMs can, in principle and in some cases in practice, have internal states and outputs that are referentially grounded, thus solving the Vector Grounding Problem and possessing intrinsic meaning independently of human interpretation.
papers.key_findings:
Distinguishes referential grounding from other forms (sensorimotor, relational, communicative, epistemic) and argues referential grounding is the only kind essential to solving the Vector Grounding Problem.
Proposes that referential grounding requires two conditions derived from teleosemantic theories: causal-informational relations to the world and a history of selection that endows internal states with the function of carrying this information.
Argues that post-training (e.g., preference tuning for factual accuracy) can establish selection processes that confer world-involving representational functions to LLM internal states.
Suggests that pre-training might, under specific conditions, also lead to world-involving representational functions through implicit extra-linguistic success conditions in the training data.
Contends that in-context learning could, in principle, allow LLMs to acquire world-involving representational functions during inference without parameter updates.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) produce seemingly meaningful outputs, yet they are trained on text alone without direct interaction with the world. This leads to a modern variant of the classical symbol grounding problem in AI: can LLMs' internal states and outputs be about extra-linguistic reality, independently of the meaning human interpreters project onto them? We argue that they can. We first distinguish referential grounding -- the connection between a representation and its worldly referent -- from other forms of grounding and argue it is the only kind essential to solving the problem. We contend that referential grounding is achieved when a system's internal states satisfy two conditions derived from teleosemantic theories of representation: (1) they stand in appropriate causal-informational relations to the world, and (2) they have a history of selection that has endowed them with the function of carrying this information. We argue that LLMs can meet both conditions, even without multimodality or embodiment.

papers.title: Causality is Key for Interpretability Claims to Generalise
papers.research_question: How can interpretability claims be made more rigorous and generalizable? The paper argues that causal inference specifies what constitutes a valid mapping from model activations to invariant high-level structures and the evidence needed to support such claims.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a causal framework for interpretability, arguing that claims should be stated in the language of causal inference and identifiability to ensure they generalize. It uses Pearl's causal hierarchy to diagnose claim-evidence mismatches and causal representation learning to specify assumptions.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability claims should be grounded in causal inference to ensure they generalize, and practitioners should use a causal framework to align methods, evidence, and claims.
papers.key_findings:
There is a frequent gap between the evidence provided by interpretability methods (e.g., associational) and the strength of the claims made (e.g., interventional or counterfactual).
A pilot study of 50 papers found roughly half of interpretability claims can admit a stronger interpretation than the evidence supports, indicating a field-wide terminological challenge.
papers.abstract: Interpretability research on large language models (LLMs) has yielded important insights into model behaviour, yet recurring pitfalls persist: findings that do not generalise, and causal interpretations that outrun the evidence. Our position is that causal inference specifies what constitutes a valid mapping from model activations to invariant high-level structures, the data or assumptions needed to achieve it, and the inferences it can support. Specifically, Pearl's causal hierarchy clarifies what an interpretability study can justify. Observations establish associations between model behaviour and internal components. Interventions (e.g., ablations or activation patching) support claims how these edits affect a behavioural metric (\eg, average change in token probabilities) over a set of prompts. However, counterfactual claims -- i.e., asking what the model output would have been for the same prompt under an unobserved intervention -- remain largely unverifiable without controlled supervision. We show how causal representation learning (CRL) operationalises this hierarchy, specifying which variables are recoverable from activations and under what assumptions. Together, these motivate a diagnostic framework that helps practitioners select methods and evaluations matching claims to evidence such that findings generalise.

papers.title: Thinking About Thinking: SAGE-nano's Inverse Reasoning for Self-Aware Language Models
papers.research_question: How can large language models be enabled to introspect on and explain their own reasoning processes, specifically why they choose particular reasoning chains over alternatives?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces inverse reasoning, a paradigm enabling LLMs to introspect on their own reasoning processes via attention pathway reconstruction, and presents SAGE-nano, a 4B-parameter model that demonstrates this capability, improving both reasoning transparency and performance.
papers.conclusion: The inverse reasoning paradigm enables LLMs to introspect on their reasoning and generate interpretable explanations, enhancing transparency and trustworthiness while maintaining competitive performance, establishing foundations for transparent AI systems in safety, education, and scientific discovery.
papers.key_findings:
SAGE-nano achieves competitive reasoning accuracy (e.g., 74.6% on AQUA-RAT) and high explanation quality (92.1% human preference score).
Inverse reasoning enhances both reasoning transparency and forward reasoning performance, as shown by ablation studies.
The model demonstrates superior introspection accuracy in identifying decision points, alternative paths, and confidence calibration.
The architecture can be trained and deployed efficiently on consumer hardware (Mac Mini M1 cluster), making advanced reasoning more accessible.
Inverse reasoning addresses critical AI safety challenges by providing interpretable explanations of model decision-making.
papers.limitation:
The inverse reasoning approach adds significant computational overhead (40% inference time), limiting scalability to larger models.
Current metrics for explanation quality rely heavily on subjective human evaluation; developing automated evaluation metrics remains an open problem.
Inverse reasoning explanations lack objective ground truth, making validation difficult.
The 4-billion parameter constraint limits the model's capacity for complex reasoning tasks compared to larger state-of-the-art models.
future_direction: Investigating inverse reasoning capabilities in larger model architectures (scalability studies).
Extending inverse reasoning to visual and multi-modal reasoning tasks.
Developing robust automated metrics for explanation quality assessment.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities at solving complex reasoning tasks with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, but their decision-making processes remain somewhat blackbox. We introduce textbfinverse reasoning, a novel paradigm enabling LLMs to decompose and explain their own reasoning chains post-hoc. Our approach, used in SAGE-nano, a 4-billion-parameter reasoning model, employs a metacognitive structure that reflects back via attention processes to identify major decision points and generate explanations of reasoning choices. While typical CoT approaches are directed towards forward reasoning generation, inverse reasoning provides insight into why specific reasoning chains were selected over others. Through thorough testing of logical reasoning puzzles, math problems and ethical dilemmas from AQUA-RAT, CommonsenseQA, and customized benchmarks, we demonstrate that SAGE-nano is at the cutting edge both on reasoning accuracy (74.6% on AQUA-RAT) and explanation quality (92.1% human preference score) for its task, and offers performance almost on par with models like Claude-3.5 Sonnet or GPT-4o. Our contributions are: (i) the first rigorous framework for LLM self-reflection via inverse reasoning, (ii) a novel metalearning framework to reverse the attention flow, (iii) comprehensive evaluation frameworks for reasoning transparency, and (iv) evidence that increasing reasoning using inverse reasoning improves interpretability along with reasoning performance. Our work creates new avenues for transparent AI systems and closes significant gaps in AI safety, education, and scientific discovery.

papers.title: Logical Phase Transitions: Understanding Collapse in LLM Logical Reasoning
papers.research_question: How does logical reasoning performance in LLMs change with increasing logical complexity? Does it degrade smoothly or collapse abruptly at critical thresholds?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Logical Complexity Metric (LoCM) and discovers Logical Phase Transitions (LPTs) in LLM reasoning, then proposes Neuro-Symbolic Curriculum Tuning to mitigate reasoning collapse at high logical complexity.
papers.conclusion: Logical Phase Transitions are a fundamental phenomenon in LLM reasoning, and Neuro-Symbolic Curriculum Tuning effectively mitigates reasoning collapse, improving performance and generalization across logical complexity levels.
papers.key_findings:
Logical reasoning performance in LLMs collapses abruptly beyond critical complexity thresholds, termed Logical Phase Transitions.
The proposed Logical Complexity Metric (LoCM) quantifies logical difficulty and reveals phase transitions.
Neuro-Symbolic Curriculum Tuning, which aligns natural language and symbolic representations and uses complexity-aware curriculum, mitigates reasoning collapse and improves generalization.
The method achieves average accuracy gains of +1.26 in naive prompting and +3.95 in CoT across five benchmarks.
Phase transitions are universal across open- and closed-source LLMs.
future_direction: Complexity-aware curriculum learning for reinforcement learning.
Process-level supervision via verifiable symbolic reasoning chains.
LoCM as a diagnostic tool for reasoning robustness.
papers.abstract: Symbolic logical reasoning is a critical yet underexplored capability of large language models (LLMs), providing reliable and verifiable decision-making in high-stakes domains such as mathematical reasoning and legal judgment. In this study, we present a systematic analysis of logical reasoning under controlled increases in logical complexity, and reveal a previously unrecognized phenomenon, which we term Logical Phase Transitions: rather than degrading smoothly, logical reasoning performance remains stable within a regime but collapses abruptly beyond a critical logical depth, mirroring physical phase transitions such as water freezing beyond a critical temperature threshold. Building on this insight, we propose Neuro-Symbolic Curriculum Tuning, a principled framework that adaptively aligns natural language with logical symbols to establish a shared representation, and reshapes training dynamics around phase-transition boundaries to progressively strengthen reasoning at increasing logical depths. Experiments on five benchmarks show that our approach effectively mitigates logical reasoning collapse at high complexity, yielding average accuracy gains of +1.26 in naive prompting and +3.95 in CoT, while improving generalization to unseen logical compositions. Code and data are available at https://github.com/AI4SS/Logical-Phase-Transitions.

papers.title: The Logical Implication Steering Method for Conditional Interventions on Transformer Generation
papers.research_question: How to leverage concept vectors to build logical implication into pre-trained transformer models, enabling transparent and interpretable adjustments to induce generation behavior in response to concepts.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Logical Implication Model Steering (LIMS) method, which uses concept vectors to program logical implication into pre-trained transformer models for interpretable behavior steering.
